chapters.title: Chapter 3: Fixed Income and Rates Through the Cycle

lessons.title: The RBI Rate Cycle and Bond Prices: The Basic Mechanics

body.text: Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions, always. Once that one fact is wired into your head, the RBI's rate decisions translate directly into what happens to every bond fund NAV you own.

children.text: Chapter 2 showed how equities react to the growth-inflation dials in ways that involve sentiment, sector positioning, and valuation judgement. Fixed income reacts to the same dials too, but through a far more mechanical, formula-driven relationship. This lesson builds the one mechanic you need before anything else in this chapter makes sense: how RBI rate moves turn into bond price moves.
The One Rule That Explains Almost Everything About Bonds

markDefs.definition: The fixed periodic interest payment a bond pays, set as a percentage of its face value when it is issued. A 7% coupon on a ₹1,000 face value bond pays ₹70 a year, regardless of what happens to interest rates later.
The return an investor earns if they buy a bond today at its current market price and hold it to maturity, factoring in both the coupon and any difference between the purchase price and face value.

children.text: set at issuance. Once it starts trading, its price moves so that its effective

stays in line with whatever new bonds are offering. If new bonds start offering 8% and your old bond still only pays a 7% coupon, nobody will pay full face value for it, its price has to fall until its effective yield to a new buyer also works out to about 8%. That single adjustment mechanism is why bond prices and yields always move in opposite directions.

A bond's price is simply the present value of all its future cash flows, the coupons plus the face value at maturity, discounted at the current market yield. That is the same present-value logic from the growth-versus-value lesson, applied to a fixed, known set of cash flows instead of an uncertain, growing one.

body.caption: Same bond, same 1-percentage-point yield rise (7% to 8%), different maturities: ₹1,000 face value, 7% annual coupon

body.text: This is exactly the duration effect from the last chapter's growth-versus-value lesson, now applied to actual bonds instead of a single distant cash flow. The same 1-percentage-point yield rise costs a 10-year bond over three-and-a-half times more, in price terms, than it costs a 2-year bond. Longer maturity means higher duration, for bonds just as much as for growth stocks.

children.text: How the Repo Rate Reaches the Rest of the Yield Curve

markDefs.definition: The rate at which the RBI lends short-term money to commercial banks against government securities. It is the RBI's main policy tool and the anchor for short-term interest rates across the economy.

children.text: The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meets roughly every two months, six times a year, to set the

. A repo rate change moves short-term money market rates and short-dated government securities almost immediately, since they are anchored tightly to it. The 10-year G-Sec yield, the benchmark long bond, is looser: it also reflects the market's inflation expectations, the government's borrowing programme for the year, and global bond yields, so it can drift ahead of or behind the RBI's actual moves.

Facing inflation running well above its comfort zone, the RBI raised the repo rate from 4.00% to 6.50% between May 2022 and February 2023, across six increases over about nine months, the clearest recent example of a full tightening cycle.

stats.label: 10-year G-Sec yield, mid-2022

body.text: Notice the 10-year G-Sec yield had already jumped well before the RBI finished hiking. Bond markets, like equity markets, are forward looking: professional bond investors were pricing in the hikes they expected the RBI to make, not waiting for each one to actually happen. This is the same leading-indicator behaviour from Chapter 1, now showing up in the debt market.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: The RBI cuts the repo rate at its next policy meeting. All else equal, what should happen to the price of an existing long-dated government bond you hold?
options: Its price is unaffected by RBI policy
It depends only on the bond's face value
body.explanation: A rate cut generally pulls yields down. Since bond prices and yields move in opposite directions, a fall in yields pushes the price of an existing bond up, and the effect is larger for longer-dated bonds, which carry more duration.

body.title: Calculate It Yourself
body.prompt: A 5-year bond has a ₹1,000 face value and a 7% annual coupon, currently priced at par because its yield is also 7%. If its yield rises to 8%, by approximately what percentage does its price fall? Enter a positive number.
body.explanation: This matches the 5-year row in the table above: price falls from ₹1,000 to about ₹960, a fall of roughly 4%, sitting between the smaller move for the 2-year bond and the larger move for the 10-year bond.

body.text: Don't assume the 10-year G-Sec yield moves one-for-one, or even in the same direction at the same time, as the repo rate. It can rise ahead of hikes on inflation fears, or stay stubbornly high even after cuts if the government's borrowing programme is large or global yields are rising. The repo rate anchors the short end of the curve directly; the long end has a mind of its own, a theme the next two lessons build on.

body.text: Bond price calculations in this lesson use simplified annual-coupon assumptions and rounded yields for teaching purposes; real bonds often pay semi-annual coupons and trade at prices that reflect additional factors like accrued interest and liquidity. Rate and yield figures are rounded and approximate. Nothing here is investment advice; consult a SEBI registered investment adviser for advice on your own portfolio.

points: Bond prices and yields always move in opposite directions, because a bond's price adjusts so its effective yield stays in line with what new bonds are offering
A bond's price is the present value of all its future coupons plus its face value, discounted at the current market yield
The same yield change hits longer-maturity bonds much harder than shorter ones: a 1-percentage-point rise cost a 10-year bond about 6.7% in this lesson's example, versus about 1.8% for a 2-year bond

The RBI's repo rate, set by the MPC roughly every two months, anchors short-term rates almost immediately, while the 10-year G-Sec yield also reflects inflation expectations, government borrowing, and global yields

In the 2022-23 hiking cycle, the RBI raised the repo rate from 4.00% to 6.50% over about nine months, but the 10-year G-Sec yield had already jumped well before several of those hikes actually happened, a leading-indicator effect
Never assume the long end of the yield curve moves in lockstep with the repo rate; it frequently doesn't, which is exactly what the next two lessons dig into
